boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's Wertingen entry (8 October 1805), the first action of the Ulm campaign in cohort v1's third-coalition 1805 group; Günzburg (B363b) follows on 9 October. Side A is Murat's reserve cavalry with Lannes's 5th corps, side B Auffenberg's division of Werneck's corps. The pursuit after dark and the next day's movements are context. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side A (French) 7,000 cavalry ('Reiter') under Murat and side B (Austrian) 9 battalions and 2 squadrons, 8,000 men, under Auffenberg. By his stated rule these are the forces available for the engagement, not only those that fought, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several (scoping decision 1). 'Reiter' counts cavalry only, so the entry gives no French infantry. No moment is stated. English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'.

claims.value: Krauss (Austrian) puts side B, Auffenberg's division, at about 5,000 infantry and 400 cavalry, calculated from the strength return of 6 October. A captured officer gave it 6 guns, the French claimed to have taken 10, and its establishment called for 18; Krauss says the number it actually had cannot be established.
claims.rationale: Side B's own figure, from an Austrian general's history based on the Kriegsarchiv files; the return itself was not inspected. The return predates the order of battle of 7 October that changed the division's composition (claim krauss-side-b-composition), and Krauss does not say how he carried it forward. English rendering (ours): 'The strength of Auffenberg's division amounted, calculated from the return of 6 October, to about 5000 infantry and 400 horse; according to a captured officer it had 6 guns, the French claimed to have captured 10 guns, and by its organisation the division should have had 18 guns' ... 'it cannot be established how many guns the division really had with it'.

English rendering (ours): 'On 6 October his division consisted of the infantry regiments Reuß-Greitz, Württemberg and Spork and the light-horse regiment Latour; with the order of battle of 7 October seven grenadier battalions took the place of the regiments Spork and Württemberg, and four and a half squadrons of Albert cuirassiers that of the regiment Latour.'

claims.value: French documents describe side B as follows. A captured Hungarian officer, questioned by Compans: 9 battalions (7 grenadier, 2 fusilier), 2 'divisions' of cuirassiers and 6 six-pounder guns. The journal of the 1st dragoon division: a corps of 12,000 men, mostly grenadiers. Alombert and Colin's narrative: 7 grenadier battalions, 2 fusilier battalions and 4 squadrons of cuirassiers.
claims.rationale: Side A's statements about side B, kept separate from side B's own figure. The journal's 12,000 is an estimate made at the time and far above Krauss's return-based figure; the prisoner and the narrative agree on 9 battalions. All figures read from page images. English renderings (ours): p. 329, 'the corps of Austrian troops that defended Wertingen was composed of 9 battalions, 7 of them grenadiers and 2 fusiliers; of 2 divisions of cuirassiers and of 6 guns of calibre 6'; p. 318, 'where the enemy had a corps of 12,000 men, most of them grenadiers'; p. 29, 'the Austrian division, which comprised 7 battalions of grenadiers, 2 of fusiliers and 4 squadrons of cuirassiers'.

claims.value: Krauss puts side A at about 8,000 infantry and 6,000 cavalry with 21 guns, of which only part fought: of the cavalry only the two dragoon divisions and the light cavalry of Lannes's corps, about 4,000 horse, and of Oudinot's division probably only the leading battalions.
claims.rationale: An Austrian-side figure for side A, kept separate. Krauss's preface says his history rests on the orders and letters of Napoleon and his marshals printed by Alombert and Colin and on the Kriegsarchiv files, so this figure is not independent of French records. English rendering (ours): 'The strength of the French amounted on the other hand to about 8000 infantry and 6000 horse with 21 guns. Only part of this force came into the fight: of the cavalry only the two dragoon divisions and the light cavalry of Lannes's corps fought, that is about 4000 horse; of Oudinot's division too only the leading battalions can have come into action.'

claims.value: Side A's returns at the crossing of the Rhine, in the first days of vendémiaire year XIV (late September 1805), give these figures for the formations at Wertingen. 5th corps (Lannes): the 1st division of grenadiers and voltigeurs, 10 battalions and 7,048 men; the light cavalry, 12 squadrons with 1,349 men and 1,393 troop horses (printed subtotal). Cavalry reserve: the 1st dragoon division, 18 squadrons with 2,489 men and 2,362 horses; the 3rd dragoon division, 18 squadrons with 2,280 men and 2,140 horses; the 1st heavy cavalry division, 18 squadrons with 3,208 men and 2,732 horses. Figures without a printed subtotal are our sums of the printed rows. The returns' totals are headed 'présents sous les armes' (present under arms).
claims.rationale: Side A's own figures, read from the page images; they are some two weeks older than the action and show neither the losses of the march nor detachments. Identification of the formations: Berthier writes that Lannes attacked with 'the grenadiers forming his first division', and Alombert and Colin call them Oudinot's grenadiers; Krauss says the light cavalry of Lannes's corps fought. The 1st dragoon division's journal names Klein as its general and puts the 3rd dragoon division and 'the 1st of cuirassiers' in the same column; Alombert and Colin have Murat marching with the divisions Klein, Beaumont and Nansouty, and Beaumont's division included the 9th dragoons (OCR), which the return places in the 3rd dragoon division. We take 'the 1st of cuirassiers' to be the return's 1st heavy cavalry division; no passage read names its commander. By Krauss only the two dragoon divisions and Lannes's light cavalry fought among the cavalry (claim krauss-side-a-strength). The horse figures of the cavalry reserve page as read fall 5 short of its printed subtotal, so one of them may be misread (transcription note). English renderings (ours): '5th army corps at the crossing of the Rhine in the first days of vendémiaire year XIV'; '1st division (grenadiers and voltigeurs)'; 'light cavalry'; 'total of those present under arms'; 'cavalry reserve at the crossing of the Rhine in the first days of vendémiaire year XIV'; '1st dragoon division'; '3rd dragoon division'; '1st heavy cavalry division'; 'Marshal Lannes, with the grenadiers forming his first division'; 'Oudinot's grenadiers'; Krauss, 'of the cavalry only the two dragoon divisions and the light cavalry of Lannes's corps fought'; 'marches and historical reports of the 1st division of mounted dragoons'; 'at 9 o'clock it received the order to form the advance guard of a column composed of the 3rd dragoon division and the 1st of cuirassiers'; 'General Klein, wishing to attack the enemy outposts, had 60 dragoons dismount, taken from the three regiments of the 1st brigade'; 'with the divisions Klein, Beaumont, Nansouty'; 'Murat orders the 9th dragoons, of Beaumont's division'.

claims.value: Napoleon's orders of 8 October, through Berthier, sent Murat with the three dragoon divisions and the two heavy cavalry divisions toward Zusmarshausen and Burgau, and sent Lannes with his corps to occupy Wertingen; Berthier authorised Murat to take two regiments of Lannes's cavalry division to scout for his heavy cavalry. Murat marched with the divisions Klein, Beaumont and Nansouty, with General Treilhard's hussar brigade (9th and 10th hussars) as advance guard from Mertingen, placed under his orders by the Emperor; d'Hautpoul's division was far behind. Saint-Hilaire's division, whose support Murat asked for, reached neither Wertingen nor Augsburg.
claims.rationale: The French official history and the orders it prints. In the passages read Lannes was ordered to Wertingen by the Emperor and was not placed under Murat. The number of the corps Treilhard's brigade came from is illegible in the OCR ('#°'). English renderings (ours): 'Marshal Lannes will leave during the day with his army corps and will occupy Wertingen'; 'the Emperor's intention is that with the three divisions of dragoons and the two divisions of heavy cavalry ... you move on Zusmarshausen and Burgau. Marshal Lannes's cavalry division marching in the same direction, you are authorised to take two regiments of it to scout the march of your heavy cavalry'; 'the advance guard is formed, from Mertingen, by the hussar brigade of the [illegible] corps (General Treilhard, 9th and 10th hussars), which is placed under Murat's orders by the Emperor'; Saint-Hilaire 'in the end arrived neither at the combat of Wertingen nor at Augsburg'.

claims.value: On the field Murat ordered the troops forward once the enemy's position had been reconnoitred, and sent the 9th dragoons of Beaumont's division through the village at the gallop; Krauss says Murat later ordered the 3rd dragoon division to attack through Wertingen. The 1st dragoon division's journal says its commander, Klein, seeing the enemy trying to withdraw, conceived the plan of cutting off its retreat, and the division went by Roggden to turn the Austrians from the south. Lannes, hearing the first cannon shots, pressed his column forward and went ahead himself, and with Fauconnet's chasseur brigade and Oudinot's division tried to slip behind the Austrians along the woods. Krauss says it was the intention of both French leaders to envelop the enemy on all sides.
claims.rationale: Decisions as the French official history, the journal it prints and Krauss attribute them. Lannes acted on hearing the guns, not on an order from Murat in the passages read, and the journal credits the turning move to Klein, so decisions on side A were taken by two marshals and a division commander; Bodart names Murat alone. English renderings (ours): 'the enemy's position having been well reconnoitred, His Serene Highness ordered the troops to move'; 'Murat orders the 9th dragoons, of Beaumont's division, to cross the village at the gallop to charge whatever it found at the exit'; Krauss, 'Murat gave the 3rd dragoon division the order to advance to the attack through Wertingen'; 'General Klein, who saw from the enemy's movements that he was trying to withdraw by the heights and woods to the left of Wertingen, conceived the plan of cutting off his retreat'; 'pressing the march of his column, and going forward himself, he came within a few moments in sight of Wertingen'; 'Klein's division headed for Roggden to turn the Austrians from the south; at the same time Lannes was trying to slip behind them, along the woods, with his brigade of chasseurs à cheval (Fauconnet) and Oudinot's division'; Krauss: 'It was thus the intention of both French leaders to envelop the enemy from all sides.'

claims.value: Krauss says Auffenberg's division belonged to Werneck's corps and was sent to Wertingen by Mack, whose order to him has not survived. GM Count Hohenfeld, commanding the grenadier brigade, deployed battalions on the report of the enemy's approach, and GM Dienersberg led a detachment to Pfaffenhofen. The captured Hungarian officer also named Auffenberg as the corps's commander.
claims.rationale: Command chain from Krauss, who used the Kriegsarchiv files including Auffenberg's relation, and the prisoner's statement printed by the French official history. English renderings (ours): 'He came to Wertingen and apparently waited for the rest of Werneck's corps'; 'The order Mack gave him has unfortunately not been preserved'; 'on the report of the enemy's approach (when it arrived cannot be established), GM Count Hohenfeld, the commander of the grenadier brigade, placed'; 'a detachment ... under GM Dienersberg to Pfaffenhofen, to drive the enemy out'; p. 329, 'this corps, commanded by lieutenant general Auffenberg'.

claims.value: Krauss says Auffenberg, on arriving, had a grenadier battalion occupy each of the town's three gates and rested the other battalions in its streets; he issued no disposition for an enemy attack, sent Dienersberg's detachment to drive the French out of Pfaffenhofen, and, when Oudinot's division threatened, withdrew all his troops to the heights southwest of Wertingen to keep his retreat open.
claims.rationale: Krauss's account of Auffenberg's own decisions, partly from Auffenberg's relation. English renderings (ours): 'had the three gates of the town each occupied at once by a grenadier battalion; the other seven battalions were drawn up in the streets of the town and rested'; 'FML Auffenberg issued no disposition for the case of an enemy attack'; 'the threatening approach of Oudinot's division moved Auffenberg, who wanted to keep his retreat open, to withdraw all troops to the heights southwest of Wertingen'.

claims.value: Krauss says the division's task cannot be established: it was pushed forward to Wertingen as an advance guard on news of the coming French crossing at Donauwörth, without a definite purpose, and holding Wertingen was not its task. Under the operations plan of 7 October a strong advance guard at Wertingen was to make the bridges from Günzburg to the mouth of the Lech unusable and link up with Kienmayer, but Krauss thinks Auffenberg did not receive that task. The captured officer said the corps was bound for Donauwörth. Murat reported on the 8th that all his information showed the enemy retreating on Augsburg by Zusmarshausen and that Auffenberg was charged with flanking this march.
claims.rationale: Krauss's reading of the Austrian files, the prisoner's statement and Murat's inference differ; none is the lost order itself. English renderings (ours): 'the task intended for the division cannot therefore be established'; 'pushed forward to Wertingen as an advance guard, without a definite, clear intention'; 'for holding Wertingen was not his task either'; 'by the operations plan of the morning of 7 October' ... 'a strong advance guard was to be pushed forward to Wertingen, which was to make all the bridges from Günzburg to the mouth of the Lech unusable and establish contact with Kienmayer. Auffenberg, however, seems not to have received this task'; 'it was destined to go to Donauwörth'; 'all the information I have gathered announces that the enemy is retreating on Augsburg by Zusmarshausen' ... claims.value: Side A attacked. Belliard writes that Murat attacked the enemy at once on meeting him at Wertingen. The French drove in the outposts at Gottmannshofen, seized the Zusam bridge and fought into the town, and attacked the Austrian battalions from Wertingen and Roggden at once as they fell back to the heights.
claims.rationale: Both sides' sources describe the French as attacking a force that stood at Wertingen. Napoleon's orders sent Lannes to occupy Wertingen (claim side-a-objectives), but the passages show Murat ordering the advance once the position was reconnoitred and attacking at once (claim side-a-decisions), so the posture is tagged commander_created. English renderings (ours): 'the Prince attacked him at once, the enemy put up much resistance'; 'the hussars, supported by artillery, drove off the outposts standing at Gottmannshofen, which fell back on Wertingen'; 'dragoons had dismounted and were seizing the bridge of Wertingen'; 'so it came about that the Austrian battalions, in the act of falling back, were attacked simultaneously from Wertingen and from Roggden'.

open_questions: Deferred: Auffenberg's relation and Archduke Ferdinand's report of 8 October (Krauss's Beilage 6), which Krauss paraphrases for Austrian losses. Loss and prisoner figures in Murat's report (p. 316), Belliard's letter (p. 317), Alombert and Colin's narrative (p. 28) and Krauss (p. 340) were seen only in the OCR and not read from the page images, so they are not recorded.

Most consequential gap: side A's own headcount of the force present on 8 October. The targeted follow-up found the returns at the crossing of the Rhine (t. II, claim side-a-return), about two weeks older than the action; a return nearer 8 October or Murat's detailed report could narrow them, and a passage naming Nansouty's division would settle which heavy cavalry division was present.

Battalion and squadron counts: Krauss's narrative (OCR, pp. 337-338, numbers in words, not read from the image) puts a grenadier battalion at each of three gates and seven more battalions in the streets, which with his footnote suggests ten battalions (the three-battalion regiment Reuß-Greitz and seven grenadier battalions), while the prisoner, Alombert and Colin and Bodart give nine. For cavalry Bodart gives 2 squadrons, the prisoner 2 'divisions', Alombert and Colin 4 squadrons and Krauss four and a half.

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his sources for this entry were not checked); Alombert and Colin, t. II and t. III (the French official history, printing French returns, orders, reports and journals); Krauss (an Austrian history from the Kriegsarchiv files, which draws on Alombert and Colin for French movements, so his French figures are not independent of theirs).
